title: Legopolitics: Toying with the Enemy — Ludic Framing in Pro-Iranian Wartime Propaganda
summary: How does war propaganda change when it looks like a toy? We study 363 pro-Iranian LEGO-style videos, tracing who gets agency, who receives blame, and whose suffering is shown. The playful format combines selective depictions of violence with references to an adversary’s own politics and popular culture.
question: How do LEGO-style wartime videos distribute agency, blame, and suffering, and how does their language differ from Iranian state media?
findings: Iranian actors occupy the agent role in 65.6% of 1,045 directed confrontations. Of 691 blame attributions directed at either named U.S. leaders or the public, 93.1% target leaders, overwhelmingly Trump; excluding Trump leaves an imprecise 52.5% share, no longer distinguishable from parity.

Within the same video and comparable target types, Iranian-inflicted violence is depicted with 0.77 standard deviations less victim suffering. This measures what the animations show, rather than real-world casualties or audience responses.

Humor is associated with views across channels, but there is no reliable association among comparable videos within the same channel. The study does not establish that humor causes circulation or persuasion.

Video text contains more U.S. domestic-political and popular-cultural references than the state-media comparison, an adjusted difference of 9.7 percentage points. Sacred legitimation is not uniformly reduced: it is especially prominent in the regime-linked core.
limitations: Interpretive scene labels come from an LLM. Independent computer-vision checks validate some concrete objects more successfully than subjective narrative judgments such as suffering or responsibility.
The discoverable-video sample omits deleted and less visible material; provenance categories do not establish direct state control.
The five-outlet state-media baseline is temporally unmatched, and engagement totals are collection-time snapshots rather than causal measures of audience effects.
sourceBasis: Complete 65-page public SSRN PDF (ssrn-7667619.pdf), including methods, all hypothesis tests, robustness tables, discussion, and appendices. Primary sample: 363 war-period videos, 7,288 scenes and 96,530 sampled frames; five historical reference videos excluded from the main sample. Source pages below use 1-based PDF pages. Figures depicting LEGO-style videos contain AI-generated study material, not website design illustrations.

summary: A game can make a historical building instantly recognizable while changing its geometry and details. We compare architecture in Assassin’s Creed, Age of Empires, and Battlefield using global image similarity, local feature matching, a vision-language model, and human ratings. Their disagreements reveal how much an “accuracy” score depends on what is being measured.
question: Do computer-vision measures and human raters agree about the architectural fidelity of historical video games?
findings: In the matched main sample of 161 architectural objects, pooled standardized scores place Battlefield 0.778 units below Assassin’s Creed, while Age of Empires is close to Assassin’s Creed. These are observational comparisons of sampled depictions, not causal effects of game design.

The methods can reverse a franchise comparison: DINOv2 rates Age of Empires above Assassin’s Creed, whereas LightGlue rates it below. Global resemblance and local geometric correspondence capture different aspects of an architectural depiction.

Gemma aligns most closely with overall human ratings (r = 0.659) in 100 image comparisons rated by four people. The automated measures are only modestly aligned with one another, and LightGlue is especially sensitive to the reference photograph.

Architectural fidelity is one part of historical representation. Neither photographic resemblance nor agreement with these raters establishes historical accuracy in a game’s narrative, society, or culture.
limitations: The image archive is selective and does not cover entire game worlds; present-day reference photographs are imperfect evidence for a structure’s appearance in a historical period.
The main analysis uses the 161 objects shared by all three model outputs, rather than every retained image or every one of the 110 reference locations.

Four raters evaluate 100 image pairs; this is neither a representative player sample nor a validation by architectural historians. Gemma’s object-level multi-reference evaluations differ in unit from the pair-level image comparisons.
sourceBasis: Complete 59-page public SSRN PDF (ssrn-6855021.pdf), dated 31 May 2026 on its title page, including sampling, model definitions, matched-sample models, human validation, robustness checks, discussion, and appendices. The downloaded archive retains 4,118 game images and 1,849 reference images across 110 locations; the shared main model sample is 161 objects / 483 model–object observations. Source pages use 1-based PDF pages. The original PDF exceeds the static host’s individual-file size limit; retain its authoritative SSRN full-text link.

summary: Can AI read a judge’s reactions from a courtroom video? We link European Court of Human Rights webcasts to judges, speakers, and judgments. An apparent difference between responses to applicants and governments largely disappears after accounting for where judges turn their heads—a lesson in measuring facial displays without mistaking them for feelings.
question: What can automated measures of facial expression reveal about judges’ courtroom behavior—and how much of the apparent signal comes from the camera?
findings: Across 311 processed recordings, the pipeline produces 372,395 verified judge-seconds. Listening-time coverage is sparse: a verified judge is visible during only 1.4% of the seconds in which a party speaks, and the three most visible judges account for 89% of listening observations.

The classifier initially assigns 3.5 percentage points more negative display during government turns than applicant turns. Accounting for head orientation reduces this to roughly 0.5–0.9 points, with intervals including zero; the raw difference largely reflects which direction judges face.

The study finds no reliable national, regional, or political-affinity differences in listening displays, but camera coverage leaves low power to detect modest effects. The null results do not establish an absence of judicial favoritism.

Facial-display measures do not improve held-out prediction of votes. Stable differences between individual faces, including demographic patterns, may reflect classifier behavior as well as expression and should not be read as judges’ inner emotions.
limitations: The outcomes are expression-classifier probabilities, not observed feelings, attitudes, or psychological states. Demographic differences cannot be separated from bias in how the classifier reads faces.
Camera placement and selective coverage strongly constrain inference. National judges appear during both parties’ turns in only 31 hearings.
Head-orientation adjustments are exploratory; human ratings of the same faces and independent replications are needed to distinguish remaining expression signals from measurement artifacts.
sourceBasis: Complete 87-page public SSRN PDF (ssrn-7712078.pdf), including all 16 hypotheses, the 311-recording data pipeline, sampling restrictions, pose analyses, specification curves, prediction tests, discussion, and appendices. Public title-page author order is Ezgi Siir Kibris followed by Cantay Caliskan. This public version supersedes the older local 11-hypothesis draft.
